extracted.intended_audience: NPR journalists and staff who use social media (reporters, editors, correspondents, social media team)
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial and ethical standards for NPR journalists' use of social media, covering conduct, verification, attribution, handling abuse, impartiality, legal risks, and internal escalation. Intended to guide day-to-day reporting and public-facing activity on social platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: conduct yourself online as you would in public
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct yourself online just as you would in any other public circumstances as an NPR journalist. Treat those you encounter online with fairness, honesty and respect, just as you would offline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent NPR in public posts; avoid actions that might discredit professional impartiality; remember you represent NPR. When in doubt, consult supervisors, Standards & Practices editor, or the Social Media Team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence: use social media as reporting and transparency tools, but with normal journalistic diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media platforms are great tools when handled correctly — valuable for newsgathering, extending contacts, speeding research and as transparency tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cite anonymous social-media posts as finished reporting; use information found there to guide reporting and attribute carefully. When referencing social media to reflect tone or mood, acknowledge it is not a scientific survey. Be guests in communities — respect cultures and do not impose. Consult Social Media Team as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect: tone and word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Words matter. Strike the right tone: be engaging and firm when necessary but never mean or abusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not SHOUT IN ALL CAPS, do not use foul language, and avoid taking the bait from trolls. Pause and re-read responses before hitting reply. There is limited room for looser language on social media if tone and intent are appropriate (example: 'badass' as a compliment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect colleagues: private criticism and sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: When posting about NPR's work, sharing colleagues' work is encouraged, but criticism of colleagues' journalism should be raised privately, not on social media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have criticism, say it to their face, not on social platforms. When using internal platforms like Slack, ask whether you'd say the same to the person's face or in front of coworkers. Respect copyrights when posting NPR work (link to story OK; copying full text/audio is not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling abusive behavior: don't feed trolls; escalate threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not respond in kind to abusive or threatening communications. 'Don't feed the trolls' and 'don't respond in kind' are guiding principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If criticism is unpleasant but non-threatening, respond with an invitation to clarify (e.g., 'I appreciate constructive feedback. Can you tell me more...?') and stop if it becomes abusive. If a message feels threatening, do not respond — forward to the internal distribution list 'NPRThreats' for Legal, Security and News Operations to review. Support is available for journalists under attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community norms and cultural awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that different online communities have their own culture, etiquette and norms; adjust behaviors appropriately while keeping ethics intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to learn platform- or community-specific norms; consult colleagues to get up to speed. Consider how conduct will affect reporting and whether adopting certain behaviors will help or harm effective reporting. Treat communities as guests would treat host cultures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy: be skeptical; add context; don't simply pass along information
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't just spread information. Be careful. Be skeptical. Add context. When pointing to what others report on social media, be thoughtful because many will view it as NPR reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about what has and hasn't been confirmed (examples of language provided). Use quote-tweet to add context and avoid appearing to endorse. Ask whether you are spreading a thinly-sourced rumor or passing on credible information with caveats. Reach out to other sources for confirmation and 'tweet/retweet as if it were going on the air or in an NPR.org story.' When in doubt, consult the Social Media Team.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about verification and sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: When using social media posts as reporting lead or source, make clear what has been confirmed and how it was checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out how information was checked and why sources are considered credible. Invite audience help in verification but do not let crowdsourcing determine reporting. Distinguish original reporting from material found on social platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up offline when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Because online identities can be faked and nuances lost, clarify and confirm information collected online through phone or in-person interviews when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a social-media posting is itself news, contact the poster/source to confirm origin and meaning. Treat online information as you would in-person leads — use follow-up to establish reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of images and video: assume inauthentic until verified
rubrics_metrics.description: Do your best to verify photos and videos posted online; when in doubt, do not publish them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Images can be manipulated or re-posted as new. Ask: When was it posted? Do the images/video match material from professionals/wire services? Is it original or a copy? Does the poster have legal right to distribute it? Seek guidance from NPR's Visuals and Social Media Teams and Legal if needed. When in doubt, leave images out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about identity and intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Be open about who you are; do not hide the fact that you work for NPR when acting in a journalistic capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use pseudonyms when doing journalistic work. You may use screen names for purely personal accounts, but you must not use information gathered under a personal identity in NPR reporting without identifying yourself to those involved and seeking permission to quote or cite them. Assume online activity can reflect on NPR even when intended as private.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online sources should be on-the-record
rubrics_metrics.description: As with in-person interviews, NPR pushes to keep virtual interactions on-the-record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make on-the-record status clear when contacting sources online. Treat information from online interactions as starting points that require follow-up reporting and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability: everything posted is public and represents NPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media outlets are public spaces; everything we write or receive is potentially visible to the public and can reflect on NPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct yourself with the expectation that you may need to defend your behavior as a journalist. Think about how choices (friends, likes, posts) will be perceived. Use privacy tools prudently but do not be complacent about their limits. When in doubt, consult supervisors or Standards & Practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality: don't advocate political issues; avoid expressing views you couldn't publish on air
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not advocate for political issues online or express personal views on political issues that you could not write for the air or post on NPR.org.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies whether posting under your name or under pseudonyms that would not readily reveal your identity. Participation in online groups can imply endorsement; consider observing rather than joining, or join openly to seek information and follow groups representing other viewpoints as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring political/advocacy groups: follow for reporting only and balance it
rubrics_metrics.description: You may follow or friend political parties and advocacy groups if doing so to keep up on what they are doing, but do so to monitor not to participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow groups from all sides of an issue. Consider whether you can accomplish goals by observing rather than joining; if you join, be transparent about purpose (seeking information/story ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal considerations and terms of service
rubrics_metrics.description: When posting or gathering material online, consider the terms of service of the social media site and legal risks, including subpoenas and permanence of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms of service may allow material to be used in ways you don't expect. Law enforcement may obtain reporting from platforms by subpoena. Even 'disappearing' platforms (e.g., Snapchat) may retain data. Be vigilant about keeping sensitive work secure and consult Legal when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retweeting and defamation risk (Section 230 nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retweeting third-party content may be protected under Section 230, but adding commentary can destroy immunity and create legal exposure for defamatory remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that simply retweeting may leave you protected in theory, but adding a defamatory remark as part of a retweet could make you liable. Be careful about repeating unverified or potentially defamatory statements, and avoid adding commentary that would make the message your own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-protection: use privacy tools but do not be complacent
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the highest level of privacy controls available to protect personal activity when appropriate, but do not rely on them as absolute protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume nothing posted privately is guaranteed private. Keep opinions guarded when appropriate and imagine posts being reported by major outlets; consider potential damage to you or NPR.
